name: have had it up to here (with X)
pattern: Clause[experiencer + perfect have had it up to here + (with + stimulus NP)]

entry.name: have had it up to here (with X)
entry.pattern: Clause[experiencer + perfect have had it up to here + (with + stimulus NP)]

1.definition: Presents the speaker or reported experiencer as having reached a limit of tolerance.
1.details: Here locates a figurative threshold. A gesture can give it a physical locus, and the idiom is also available in writing. The with-phrase can identify what has become intolerable. A literal liquid-level description lacks the experiencer and tolerance interpretation.

examples.form: We have [had it up to here with typical politicians].

projection.target: The with-phrase identifies the source of frustration. An optional height gesture can highlight the threshold, while a distance phrase does not freely substitute for here with the same idiomatic reading.
projection.evidence: The FAU records distinguish the verbal idiom from two established gesture combinations and give an example with an explicit with-phrase.

curious.title: I've had it up to here
curious.summary: Have had it up to here says someone has reached the limit of what they can put up with, and with names the cause.
curious.body: I've had it up to here doesn't describe a liquid level. It says the speaker has reached a limit of tolerance, with here marking a figurative line. A gesture can show where that line is. A with-phrase can say what has become too much: We have had it up to here with typical politicians. The expression is also available in writing, and a literal description of liquid height lacks the tolerance meaning.

examples.text: We have [had it up to here with typical politicians].

curious.try: Say I've had it up to here with ... and hold a hand at a height. Does the gesture change how strong it sounds?

teacher.summary: An idiom for reaching the limit of tolerance, with an optional with-phrase naming the cause.
teacher.explain: The idiom is perfect have plus had it up to here, optionally followed by a with-phrase: We have had it up to here with typical politicians. It presents the speaker or a reported experiencer as having reached a limit of tolerance. Here locates a figurative threshold, which a gesture can give a physical locus. The with-phrase identifies the source of frustration. A distance phrase does not freely substitute for here with the same idiomatic reading, and a literal liquid-level description lacks the experiencer and tolerance interpretation. This dictionary says the core expression has a largely fixed lexical form.
teacher.terms: Idiom is the usual word. This dictionary calls the with-phrase's referent the stimulus.

examples.text: We have [had it up to here with typical politicians].

watch_for: A learner might read it as a literal measurement of where something reaches.
A learner might replace here with a distance phrase and expect the same idiomatic reading.
A learner might leave out the perfect have, though this dictionary gives that as the canonical form.
teacher.activity: Give students a list of annoyances (a noisy neighbour, a late bus). They write I've had it up to here with ... for each, then compare a literal sentence about water height to the idiom.

child.hook: What does it mean to have had it up to here?
child.explain: This means you can't put up with something any more. A hand held up high can show where your limit is. I've had it up to here with the noise.

examples.text: [I've had it up to here with the noise].

child.play: Hold your hand up high and say you've had it up to here with something silly, like broken pencils.

checked.note: Fixed: child explanation now says a raised hand shows where your limit is, not how full you are (which could suggest food); 'the entry' replaced by 'this dictionary'.
